Family Health

Glaucoma: symptoms, eye tests and protecting your vision

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Glaucoma is a group of conditions that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It often develops without noticeable symptoms. Damage already caused by glaucoma cannot usually be reversed, but early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can help protect the vision that remains.

Why glaucoma can be difficult to notice

The common open-angle form usually progresses slowly and painlessly. Side vision may be affected before central vision, and a person may not recognise the change until considerable damage has occurred. Being able to read clearly or having no eye pain does not exclude glaucoma.

An eye examination can identify concerning changes before you notice them yourself. How often you need an examination depends on factors such as age, family history, previous findings and other risks. Ask your eye-care professional for an interval suited to you, rather than waiting for symptoms or assuming the same annual schedule fits everyone.

Sudden eye symptoms need emergency care

An acute angle-closure attack can cause severe eye pain, redness, sudden blurred or reduced vision, coloured rings around lights, nausea or vomiting. This happens when drainage is suddenly obstructed and pressure rises quickly. Seek emergency eye care immediately; do not wait for a routine appointment or try to treat it with someone else’s drops.

Not every form of angle-closure glaucoma is sudden. Some develops gradually and has few or no early symptoms. The severe symptom pattern describes the acute attack, not a checklist that everyone with glaucoma must have. Other serious eye conditions can cause similar symptoms, so an examination is essential. Do not drive yourself if your vision is affected.

How eye pressure and fluid drainage are connected

The eye continually makes a clear fluid called aqueous humour. It moves through the front chambers and drains at the angle where the iris, the coloured part of the eye, meets the clear cornea. A filtering structure called the trabecular meshwork is one of the main drainage routes. This internal fluid is different from the tears on the eye’s surface.

If drainage becomes inefficient or blocked, pressure inside the eye can rise. Over time, this may damage the optic nerve. But pressure is only part of the picture: some people have high pressure without glaucoma, while others develop glaucoma at readings within the usual range. The nerve’s condition and the visual field must also be assessed.

Open-angle and normal-tension glaucoma

In open-angle glaucoma, the drainage angle remains open, but fluid may pass through the drainage tissue too slowly. This is the most common form in many populations. It generally requires long-term monitoring because damage can continue without pain or a sudden change in sight.

Normal-tension glaucoma is an open-angle form in which optic-nerve damage occurs without pressure above the usual measured range. The reasons are not completely understood; nerve vulnerability and blood supply may contribute. Lowering eye pressure can still help. A normal pressure reading is therefore not a reason to dismiss abnormal nerve or visual-field findings.

Angle-closure and congenital glaucoma

In angle closure, the iris blocks access to the drainage angle. This can produce an acute attack or develop more slowly. A narrow angle is a finding that needs a risk assessment; it does not mean that everyone with that anatomy already has glaucoma or will need the same preventive procedure.

Congenital glaucoma involves abnormal development of the eye’s drainage system. A baby may have unusually watery eyes, sensitivity to light or a cloudy-looking cornea; the eyes may appear enlarged. These changes need prompt assessment by a pediatric eye specialist. Some forms have a genetic basis, and treatment often involves surgery. They should not be managed as a routine blocked tear duct without assessment.

Secondary glaucoma and the role of medicines

Secondary glaucoma develops in association with another problem, such as an eye injury, inflammation or certain other eye diseases. Less commonly, an advanced cataract or an eye tumour can interfere with drainage. Glaucoma may also develop after some eye operations; risk depends on the situation, and follow-up matters. These associations do not mean that every cataract or operation causes glaucoma.

Corticosteroid medicines can raise eye pressure in susceptible people. Tell the eye team about steroid drops, tablets, inhalers, creams and other medicines you use. Do not stop a prescribed steroid on your own; the prescriber and eye team can discuss the necessary treatment and monitoring.

Drops used to enlarge the pupils during an eye examination very rarely trigger an acute pressure rise in people susceptible to angle closure. This is different from saying that routine dilation commonly causes glaucoma. Tell the examiner about known narrow angles and follow the warning advice given after dilation.

Who has a higher risk?

Risk increases with age, especially in later adulthood, but glaucoma can occur earlier. Having a parent, brother or sister with glaucoma is important information for the eye-care team. Some population groups have higher rates of particular forms: open-angle disease is more common and may occur younger in people of African ancestry; angle closure is more common in some Asian populations, while normal-tension disease is reported more often in people of Japanese ancestry. These patterns guide awareness, not a diagnosis for an individual.

Past eye injury, persistent inflammation, long-term steroid exposure and certain eye characteristics can also matter. A thin central cornea is relevant to risk assessment and can affect how a pressure measurement is interpreted; it does not simply cause the pressure to rise.

Tell the clinician about diabetes, blood-pressure problems and heart or circulation conditions. These can be relevant to eye health and treatment decisions, but they do not all cause glaucoma in the same way. Do not change blood-pressure medicines to try to alter eye pressure. The eye team should consider the complete history alongside the examination.

What happens during a glaucoma assessment?

The clinician asks about symptoms, previous eye problems, family history and medicines. A comprehensive examination looks for optic-nerve damage and other explanations for changes in vision. No single pressure measurement can establish or exclude glaucoma.

Tonometry measures pressure inside the eye. Pachymetry measures corneal thickness, which helps interpret that reading. A visual-field test, also called perimetry, checks for areas of reduced vision, including around the edges. Looking at the drainage angle helps distinguish open-angle disease from angle closure.

The optic nerve may be examined through a dilated pupil, photographed or scanned with optical coherence tomography, known as OCT. Photographs and scans provide a record for comparison at later visits. Repeating tests can show whether a finding is stable or changing and whether treatment is working.

Treatment aims to preserve the sight you have

The main treatment approach is to lower eye pressure to a target chosen for the individual. That target depends on the degree of damage, how quickly it is changing and other findings. A number labelled “normal” on its own does not guarantee that the optic nerve is protected.

Prescription drops can reduce fluid production or improve drainage. Some people need more than one medicine, and tablets may be used in selected circumstances. Ask the team to check your drop technique and discuss side effects, cost or practical barriers that make regular treatment difficult. Do not wait for pain or blurred vision before using prescribed treatment.

Laser treatment may be an initial option for suitable open-angle glaucoma; it is not always reserved until drops have failed. Some laser procedures improve drainage, while other selected procedures reduce fluid production. Surgery may create an additional drainage route or use an implant when pressure needs further control. The choice depends on the type and severity of disease, likely benefits and risks, and the person’s preferences.

How an acute angle-closure attack is treated

Emergency treatment first aims to bring the pressure down quickly. Clinicians may use drops and other medicines, followed by a procedure to address the blocked flow. Laser peripheral iridotomy makes a small opening in the iris so that fluid can move more freely. It may be needed even when the initial medicines have successfully lowered the pressure.

The specialist may assess the other eye for preventive treatment and consider lens surgery or other options when appropriate. The emergency has not necessarily ended the need for follow-up or drops. The team should explain the plan and what symptoms require an urgent return.

Can glaucoma cause blindness, and can it be prevented?

Untreated or progressing glaucoma can cause permanent sight loss, including blindness. Treatment can slow or sometimes stop further damage, but it cannot restore nerve tissue already lost. Many people keep useful vision with timely care; no general article can predict the outcome for an individual eye.

There is no guaranteed way to prevent every form of glaucoma. The practical priority is timely eye assessment, monitoring known risks and continuing the treatment recommended for you. Because glaucoma is usually a long-term condition, a good pressure reading does not mean it is safe to stop treatment or skip appointments.

If vision loss affects reading, moving around or other daily tasks, ask about low-vision support and rehabilitation. Bring questions to follow-up visits: whether the tests are stable, what pressure target is being used, whether treatment needs changing and when the next check should happen.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Eye-health guidance stresses that glaucoma can be silent and can occur with pressure in the usual range. Assessment combines nerve findings, visual fields and other tests rather than relying on symptoms or one pressure reading.

Treatment is selected by glaucoma type and severity. Modern guidance includes laser as an initial option for suitable open-angle disease, while an acute angle-closure attack requires immediate care.

How BeMama can help

Keep a record of eye appointments, prescribed drops and questions for the eye team. If a family member has glaucoma, mention that history when arranging your own eye checks.

When to seek help

Sudden severe eye pain, redness with blurred vision, coloured halos or nausea and vomiting with eye symptoms need emergency assessment. Seek prompt specialist advice for a baby with cloudy eyes, marked light sensitivity or unusual tearing. Do not stop prescribed eye or steroid medicines without professional advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Glaucoma often has no early symptoms; clear central vision does not rule it out.
  • High pressure is an important risk factor, but a full eye assessment is needed.
  • An acute painful, red eye with sudden visual changes is an emergency.
  • Drops, laser and surgery aim to protect remaining vision, with ongoing follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

What are the first symptoms of glaucoma?

Often there are none. Open-angle glaucoma may gradually affect side vision without pain. Sudden severe eye pain, redness, blurred vision or nausea is a different pattern that requires emergency assessment.

Can I have glaucoma with normal eye pressure?

Yes. Normal-tension glaucoma can damage the optic nerve despite readings within the usual range. The nerve examination, visual-field results and changes over time matter as well as pressure.

Does high eye pressure mean I will go blind?

No. High pressure does not always cause glaucoma, and a glaucoma diagnosis does not make blindness inevitable. A specialist assesses the damage and risk of progression and recommends monitoring or treatment.

Can a baby have glaucoma?

Yes. Congenital glaucoma is uncommon and involves a drainage-system problem. A cloudy cornea, unusual tearing or marked light sensitivity needs prompt pediatric eye assessment rather than an assumption that it is a minor irritation.

Is glaucoma inherited?

Family history can increase risk, and some congenital forms have genetic causes. Tell the eye-care team about affected relatives. Inheritance is not the only factor, and the diagnosis still requires an examination.

Will treatment restore lost vision?

Treatment aims to stop or slow additional optic-nerve damage. Established glaucomatous nerve damage generally cannot be reversed. Low-vision services can help with practical difficulties caused by sight already lost.

Are eye drops always the first treatment?

No. Depending on the type and severity, laser, drops or surgery may be recommended. Suitable open-angle cases can receive laser early, while acute angle closure needs immediate pressure-lowering care and treatment of the obstruction.

Should I stop steroids if I am worried about glaucoma?

Do not stop them on your own. Tell the prescriber and eye specialist what you use, including inhalers and creams. They can assess whether pressure monitoring or a treatment change is appropriate.

How often should I have an eye test?

Ask for a schedule based on your age, family history, previous results and other risks. Someone with established glaucoma needs the follow-up interval set by the treating team, which may be more frequent than routine eye checks.

Can I stop my drops when the pressure improves?

An improved reading may show that treatment is working. Keep using the prescribed treatment unless the eye team changes it, and attend follow-up so that pressure, nerve structure and vision can be reassessed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
